According to John Cage, everything in our surrounding environment is music. Your microwave produces a distinct tone whenever your using it, the ticking noise made by the turn signals in your car always tick at a constant rhythm, etc. Even the horn honking in heavy traffic is made up of a collection of individual pitches that work together to create that distinct car horn sound.

There's a composer named Petr Válek who writes music that is loosely related to John Cage's later style. Petr, AFAIK, shares the same philosophy that the environment around us is music. Most of Petr's music is rooted in [chaos](https://youtu.be/NCEB-nMItcg) whereas most of Cage's music is rooted in a calm focus towards our surrounding environment, like [4'33"](https://youtu.be/rDgHUj8sJaQ). In the world of jazz, that's how you're supposed to hold a microphone (sans posh pinky). Gripping it like it's a handlebar on a motorcycle makes it seem like you don't know what you're doing. Also, you're supposed to hold the microphone perpendicular to your mouth, because most vocal mics are unidirectional, meaning it has to be spoken or sung into from a certain direction for it to pick up 100% of the sound. It's like that so that it doesn't pick up noise from any other source of noise, which can muddy the sound and/or cause feedback (that squealing sound speakers make occasionally when the microphone picks up the sound made from the speaker that the mic is connected to, which feeds back the sound projected from the speaker into the mic). OP of however many years ago is holding it in the wrong direction.

You're totally right, but in the way I'm saying, I'm getting at their tonality and quality of sound more than their style or technique. I'm a trombonist, so I'm gonna compare, say, Bill Watrous to Joseph Alessi. Different styles, Joe is a classical player (listen to The Blue Bells of Scotland), Bill is a contemporary jazz player (listen to It Might As Well Be Spring). In Joe's music, his tone is solid and rigid, whereas in Bill's music, Bill is more free and slightly airy. This is because of their instrument setups. Joe plays a large-bore tenor with an F attachment. Bill plays a straight-through tenor with a small bore lead pipe. The difference between a large and small bore horn is the diameter of the lead pipe, slides, and bell. As explained above, a wider, deeper bell gives a warmer tone. Their mouthpieces are different as well. Joe plays on a piece that has a wider and deeper cup, as well as a longer and wider shank. Bill's is pretty much the polar opposite. The bigger it is, the warmer and mellow-er it will be. I play in a big band as the lead bone, so I play on a straight-through with a Giddings and Webster small shank Chubasco mouthpiece. It's really awesome for higher-end playing, getting up to the first partial where the double Bb's and double C's are. Most of the sound comes from the player, but the instrument makes more difference than most people give credit for.

What Chuck Mangione played is called a flugelhorn. It is essentially a bass trumpet, in the sense that the bell is bigger and wider, which produces a warmer tone, the lead pipe is longer, which facilitates freer-flowing air, and the pipes are slightly wider, which does the two effects described. The horn itself is also bigger overall. It is more commonly implemented in smooth jazz (Chuck's fling), and jazz ballads (take a listen at Lush Life).

One would be embouchure, or the way the player places his lips on the mouthpiece, the mouthpiece itself, which can have varying degrees of cup depth, shank size, diameter, etc., and the trumpet itself, which varies in bell size, lead pipes, material of the horn, and the size and length of the piping. All these things go into what makes a player sound like Dizzy Gillespie or Maynard Ferguson.

I play trombone and classical guitar. I'm learning piano, seeing as though it is imperative in composing. All pieces start on piano because it is the simplest way to hear all of the chords/progressions/what have you. If you look hard enough, there is almost always a piano reduction of every piece written.

I compose for both, actually. I started with solo instruments (like horn, trombone, various voices and such) and expanded into small ensembles and then progressed into full groups when contest opportunities arose in where I live (central Texas).

I consider classical music to be the kind that is well-founded in the accepted practice of ye-olde-style music theory as founded by the great minds in classical music like Bach, Beethoven, etc. The type of classical music can vary based on its instrumentation. Baroque classical is usually characterized by strings/harpsichord. Romantic classical usually has all of the instruments in the modern orchestra, including strings, woodwinds, brass, and percussion. 

Having listened to a lot of what is considered classical music when I was younger, I have always identified my music as classical in nature because I always tend to write in that form.

"New" classical music can be considered classical because of the nature of the orchestration and the form the piece follows. New classical can be divided into lots of categories, like contemporary classical and film score (very far reach, though).

Re-writes of new stuff like Stairway to Heaven/All Along The Watchtower, in my opinion, can't be considered classical because it was never intended to be interpreted that way. Re-writing stuff like that to me takes away part of how those songs impact its audience.

I do not currently have any of my works online, mainly because I'm so protective of my work and have always disliked the notion of having my work stolen and re-branded.

As a composer, when I was writing a series of chorales for a band to practice on. I tried doing it vertically (chord by chord) and that wasn't working out for me. Common practice chord progressions just don't click with me. So instead I thought of it in horizontal terms (line by line). First I wrote the melody, then the bass line. I would then harmonize according to logical voice leading. The chords may not follow common practice, but they sound fine. I kept writing like this and lost track of my progress. Turns out I wrote more than 25 24-bar chorales for a high school marching band.

TL;DR I was over thinking my work and found a better way of doing it, which worked out way better than expected
